question: A switchboard meter uses 600:5 CTs and 4200:120 VTs. Its instrument multiplier, which ATS 7.11.1 has you verify, is:
explanation: Multiplier = CT ratio x VT ratio = 120 x 35 = 4200. A wrong multiplier makes every reading wrong even when the meter itself is accurate. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.1.B.3; IEEE 141-1993, 11.7.1.

question: Besides calibration, ATS 7.11.1 has you check what about a meter's instrument transformer circuits?
choices: That the CT secondaries are left open for safety
That the CT and VT secondary circuits are intact
That the VT fuses are bypassed during the test
That the CT ratio matches the breaker frame size
explanation: A calibrated meter on a broken secondary circuit reads nothing useful. ATS asks you to confirm the instrument transformer secondaries are complete. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.1.B.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.1.B.4

question: Before testing a microprocessor-based meter under ATS 7.11.2, which item is recorded during inspection?
choices: The CT knee-point voltage
The disk constant Kh
The ambient humidity
The firmware revision
explanation: Digital meters are inspected like small computers. ATS has you record firmware and software revisions and passwords, and then load the owner's settings. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.2.A.5.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.2.A.5

question: In IEEE C37.2-2022 terms, a remote terminal unit (RTU) in a substation is:
choices: The main interface to the SCADA master
A relay that trips breakers on loss of communication
A recorder that captures fault waveforms only
An I/O module that has no SCADA connection
explanation: C37.2 defines the RTU as the primary interface to SCADA. A remote I/O module is distinguished by having no connection to the SCADA master, and a DFR records disturbances. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.2.20 and 3.2.19.

question: A three-phase, four-wire wye service is metered. By Blondel's theorem, the number of meter elements needed for correct measurement is:
explanation: For N conductors, N - 1 properly connected elements measure the power, with the voltage coils tied to the conductor that has no current coil. Four wires need three elements. A three-wire delta needs two. Source: EEI Handbook for Electricity Metering, 11th ed., ch. 2 (Blondel's Theorem).
reference: EEI Handbook for Electricity Metering, 11th ed., ch. 2 (Blondel's Theorem)

question: A watthour meter registers 101.5 kWh while the true energy was 100.0 kWh. Its percent registration and percent error are:
choices: 98.5% registration, -1.5% error
101.5% registration, +1.5% error
100% registration, 1.5% error
1.5% registration, +101.5% error
explanation: Percent registration = registered / true x 100 = 101.5%. Percent error is the difference from 100%, so +1.5%. The meter reads high. Source: EEI Handbook for Electricity Metering, 11th ed., ch. 3 (Basic Computations Used in Metering).
reference: EEI Handbook for Electricity Metering, 11th ed., ch. 3 (Basic Computations Used in Metering)

question: A breaker status input in a SCADA RTU keeps flickering on and off many times a second because of a bad auxiliary contact. Which feature disables that point when it changes state too often?
choices: Select-before-operate
A deadband
Scan enable
A chatter filter
explanation: IEEE C37.1 defines a chatter filter as the feature that disables a digital input when it changes state too many times within a set interval. Deadband applies to analog values, and select-before-operate applies to control commands. Source: IEEE C37.1-2007, 3.1.3.

question: An electromechanical meter with Kh = 1.8 runs on 80:1 instrument transformers (combined multiplier). The disk makes 10 revolutions in 36 seconds. The primary load is:
choices: 1.8 kW
144 kW
180 kW
explanation: kW = 3.6 x revolutions x Kh x multiplier / seconds = 3.6 x 10 x 1.8 x 80 / 36 = 144 kW. Leaving out the multiplier gives 1.8 kW at the meter. Source: IEEE 141-1993, 11.7.1.

question: A 4-wire wye service is metered with a 2-element meter. What does the EEI Handbook say about this?
choices: It isn't a Blondel connection, so it can misregister
It is the correct connection, since the neutral carries no power
It is accurate as long as the CTs are 0.3 class
It reads exactly double and is corrected through the meter multiplier
explanation: Blondel's theorem needs N - 1 elements for N wires, so a 4-wire wye needs three. A 2-element (non-Blondel) arrangement depends on assumptions about balance and can register in error. Source: EEI Handbook for Electricity Metering, 11th ed., ch. 2 (Blondel's Theorem) and ch. 11.
reference: EEI Handbook for Electricity Metering, 11th ed., ch. 2 (Blondel's Theorem) and ch. 11

question: A new microprocessor meter passed its bench injection. After energization, it shows negative kW on a feeder that is clearly carrying load away from the bus. ATS 7.11.2 says:
choices: The meter passed bench calibration, so the reading is accepted
Negative kW is normal on feeders and needs no action
Repeat the bench test at a higher accuracy class
Readings must match load; check CT polarity
explanation: Calibration proves the meter, not the installed circuit. ATS has you confirm after energization that readings match the loads (per ECS). A sign reversal usually points to reversed CT polarity or a wiring error. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.2.B.3 and D.3.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.11.2.B.3 and D.3

question: An analog point in a new substation RTU doesn't update at SCADA for small load changes, but large changes come through. Which setting is behind this, and which ATS 7.23 test checks it?
choices: The chatter filter; ATS has you verify failover time
The deadband; ATS checks deadband operation
The select-before-operate timer; ATS has you verify tagging
The scan enable flag; ATS has you verify date and time
explanation: Data change detection stores a new value only when the change exceeds the deadband, so small changes are suppressed by design. ATS 7.23 includes verifying deadband and zero deadband. Source: IEEE C37.1-2007, 6.4.3.1 item b); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23.B.7.
reference: IEEE C37.1-2007, 6.4.3.1 item b); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23.B.7

question: Why does a SCADA breaker control use select-before-operate?
choices: To speed up control by skipping the confirmation step
So the right point is armed and confirmed first
To let two operators command the same breaker at the same time
To keep analog values from updating during a control
explanation: SBO is a two-part sequence. The point is selected (armed) and confirmed, then an operate command must arrive before a timer expires. The goal is to avoid operating the wrong point or more than one point. Source: IEEE C37.1-2007, 3.1.20 and Annex D.1.
reference: IEEE C37.1-2007, 3.1.20 and Annex D.1

question: Sequence-of-events records from three relays in a new substation disagree by several seconds. Which commissioning checks address this?
choices: Raise the deadband on the analog points
Clear the event buffers on each relay before every test
Increase the SCADA scan cycle
Check time synchronization and device date/time
explanation: ECS for medium voltage asks for IEDs and SCADA to be on an adequate time-sync source with correct date and time. ATS 7.23 also checks date and time and requires accurate timestamps. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 7.2.A.24; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23.A.10 and C.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 7.2.A.24; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23.A.10 and C.4

question: What is IEC 61850 GOOSE messaging used for in a substation?
choices: Billing-grade interval energy data sent to the utility once a day
Firmware upgrades over a serial port
Client/server retrieval of event files only
Fast, repeated peer-to-peer status and trip messages between IEDs
explanation: GOOSE carries status, controls, and measured values between peers on the Ethernet network. Each message is sent several times. File and report retrieval use MMS client/server services instead. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (GOOSE); IEEE C37.2-2022, Annex B.
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (GOOSE); IEEE C37.2-2022, Annex B

question: A relay's GOOSE message uses the default minimum time of 8 ms and a maximum time of 1000 ms. When a change triggers it, the repeats follow the min, min, twice-min, then max pattern. When is the fourth transmission sent, measured from the trigger?
choices: 16 ms
24 ms
32 ms
explanation: First send at 0, second 8 ms later (8), third 8 ms after that (16), fourth twice the minimum later (32 ms). After that the message repeats at the 1000 ms maximum until another change. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (GOOSE Processing).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (GOOSE Processing)

question: Which IEC 61850 SCL file describes one configured IED as it will be loaded into that device?
choices: ICD (IED capability description)
CID (configured IED description)
SSD (system specification description)
SCD (substation configuration description)
explanation: ICD lists what an IED can do. SSD describes the single-line and needed logical nodes. SCD covers the whole substation. CID is the instantiated configuration for one device. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (SCL Files).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (SCL Files)

question: In IEC 61850 logical-node names, a 51 time-overcurrent element and a 52 circuit breaker map to:
choices: PIOC and CSWI
PTOC and XCBR
PDIF and XSWI
PTOC and PIOC
explanation: C37.2 Annex D relates device numbers to logical nodes: 50 is PIOC, 51 is PTOC, 52 is XCBR, and 87 is PDIF. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, Annex D, Table D.1.
reference: IEEE C37.2-2022, Annex D, Table D.1

question: During commissioning, a subscribing SEL-751 ignores a GOOSE trip from another IED. Which publisher setting is a likely cause?
choices: The publisher's minimum retransmit time is set at 8 ms
The message uses a multicast address
The subscriber's front-panel display is off
The message is flagged Test or Needs Commissioning
explanation: The SEL-751 rejects the data in an incoming GOOSE when Test Mode or Needs Commissioning is true, the configuration number changes, or it can't decode the message. Check those flags before blaming the wiring or logic. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (incoming GOOSE processing).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Appendix G (incoming GOOSE processing)

question: IEEE C37.2 notes that managed Ethernet switches in a GOOSE-based protection scheme are, in effect:
choices: The auxiliary relays of the scheme
Passive cable connectors with no settings
Metering devices only, with no role in protection
Backup power supplies for the relays
explanation: In an Ethernet protection scheme the switch is a message-processing computer whose settings route trips and interlocks. C37.2 gives it device number 16 with the suffix ES. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, Annex B and 3.1.16.
reference: IEEE C37.2-2022, Annex B and 3.1.16

question: A microprocessor relay's setting-change alarm and protection-operate, protection-fail, and communications-fail indications are mapped to the plant SCADA system, but those points have never been tested. Component relay tests passed. What should you require?
choices: Verify the mapped SCADA points and, where the project calls for it, the setting-change alarm, and confirm that the communication paths used for those points actually work before you accept the scheme
Bench element tests prove every SCADA indication, so no further check is needed
SCADA points are the plant IT department's responsibility and are outside acceptance testing
Only a communications-fail alarm is ever tested; the other indications are cosmetic
explanation: ATS includes optional and required checks on microprocessor relays for SCADA points such as protection-operate, protection-fail, communications-fail, and fault-recorder trigger, a setting-change alarm to SCADA, and a confirmation that the communication paths actually work. Isolated element tests do not prove those points. Official IEC 61850 commissioning practice is not used here because that source is not in the held set. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.9.2.B.8, 7.9.2.B.9, and 7.9.2.B.10.

question: An IEC 61850 project has four SCL files on the server: SSD, ICD, SCD, and CID. The owner asks which file describes the configured substation automation system as a whole. What are those files, and which one answers the question?
choices: The four file types use unrelated formats, and the ICD file is the one that describes the entire substation system
SSD, ICD, SCD, and CID are interchangeable names for the same file, so any one of them describes the system

All four use the same XML format but have different scopes. The substation configuration description (SCD) describes the configured system. SSD is the system specification, ICD is the IED's capability, and CID is one IED as configured to be loaded
Only the CID file can describe the substation as a whole, because it is the only file written after the IEDs are purchased
explanation: Part 6 defines an XML substation configuration language and a family of files that share methods and format but have different scopes: the system specification description (SSD), the IED capability description (ICD), the substation configuration description (SCD), and the configured IED description (CID). Those four roles should not be treated as interchangeable filenames. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 7.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 7

question: A protection GOOSE and a sampled-value stream will share a station Ethernet network with ordinary MMS reports. What does the Adamiak overview say about how those three are mapped on the stack?
choices: GOOSE and sampled values are mapped directly into the Ethernet frame, skipping the middle layers. MMS uses a connection-oriented profile that can run over TCP/IP or ISO. GSSE, the older UCA-style event, runs over connectionless ISO services
GOOSE, sampled values, and MMS all travel as ordinary TCP/IP application traffic, with no special Ethernet mapping
Sampled values require MMS, and GOOSE requires TCP, so neither can run if the station bus has no IP routing
GSSE is the same Ethernet Ethertype mapping as GOOSE and never uses ISO connectionless services
explanation: Part 8.1 sets the lower-layer profiles, and those profiles depend on the service. GOOSE, and sampled values, are mapped straight into the Ethernet data frame. MMS client/server traffic can run over TCP/IP or ISO transport. That is a change from the older UCA GOOSE, which used connectionless ISO services. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 5 and Figure 4.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 5 and Figure 4

question: A process-bus design will digitize currents and voltages out at the yard. What device does the Adamiak overview place at that process layer, and how do IEC 61850-9-1 and 9-2 differ?
choices: A station HMI digitizes the yard quantities, and 9.1 and 9.2 are two names for the same MMS report
Part 9.2 is only a point-to-point link with a fixed dataset, while 9.1 is the multicast process bus
Merging units are used only for MMS file transfer, not for sampled values

A merging unit collects the sensor and status inputs and publishes sampled values. Part 9.1 is a unidirectional point-to-point link with a fixed dataset; part 9.2 is a configurable dataset that can be multicast from one publisher to many subscribers and is the more general process-bus implementation
explanation: The process layer gathers voltage, current, and status from the primary equipment. A merging unit takes those signals, samples them at an agreed, synchronized rate, and publishes sampled measured values so any IED can align data from more than one unit. Part 9.1 defines a unidirectional multidrop point-to-point link carrying a fixed dataset (as in IEC 60044-8). Part 9.2 defines a user-configurable dataset, described in SCL, that can be transmitted on a multicast basis from one publisher to multiple subscribers, and is the more generalized process-bus implementation. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 6.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 6

question: A merging-unit specification must state a synchronized sample rate. What two rates does the implementation agreement in the Adamiak overview record?
choices: A single rate of 16 samples per cycle is used for both protection and oscillography
80 samples in each power-system cycle for ordinary protection and monitoring, and 256 samples in each cycle when high-frequency work such as power-quality or high-resolution oscillography is required
Protection uses 256 samples per cycle, and metering uses 80 samples per cycle
The standard forbids agreeing on a sample rate; each IED may sample independently
explanation: Merging units in a station sample at an agreed, synchronized rate so an IED can align data from more than one unit. At the time of the paper, an implementation agreement set a base rate of 80 samples in each power-system cycle for ordinary protection and monitoring, and 256 samples in each cycle when high-frequency work such as power-quality or high-resolution oscillography is required. Those streams go straight to Ethernet. VLAN filtering lets a switch deliver datasets only to subscribed ports and IEDs, and clock redundancy has to be planned so a second clock can take over if the first fails. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 6.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 6

question: During a design review, someone asks why IEC 61850-8-1 maps the abstract models to MMS rather than to a simple register-based protocol. What reason does the overview give?
choices: MMS is required because it is the only protocol that can carry raw sampled values in a process bus

MMS is a public ISO protocol with a proven record that can support the complex named objects and rich services of the IEC 61850 model, so the mapping stays straightforward. Mapping the same model onto a protocol that only offers simple read and write of register numbers would be cumbersome
IEC 61850 forbids the use of MMS; the overview recommends mapping only to Modbus registers
MMS is used only for file transfer; all operational data must use DNP3
explanation: The abstract object and service models have to run over a real, practical protocol. Part 8.1 maps them to the Manufacturing Message Specification (MMS, ISO 9506). MMS was kept from the earlier UCA work because it is the only public ISO protocol with a proven implementation record that can readily support the complex naming and service models. The same models could, in theory, be mapped to other protocols, but the mapping becomes complex when the target only provides simple read, write, and report services for variables addressed by register or index numbers. Logical devices map to MMS domains, and many other IEC 61850 classes map to named MMS variables. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 5 and Tables 2 and 3.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 5 and Tables 2 and 3

question: You are walking a new IED's logical-node list and need to know, from the name alone, whether a node is switchgear, a measurement unit, or a protection function. Which prefix rules does the overview give?
choices: Every protection function is named XCBR, and every breaker is named MMXU
Logical-node names are vendor-specific and have no standard first-letter assignment
The first letter is only an instance number; the function is carried only in a comment field

Protection logical nodes begin with P, switchgear with X (XCBR is a circuit breaker), instrument transformers with T, power transformers with Y, and metering and measurement with M (MMXU is a three-phase measurement unit)
explanation: IEC 61850-7-4 groups logical nodes by a standard first letter: A for automatic control, M for metering and measurement, C for supervisory control, G for generic functions, I for interfacing and archiving, L for system logical nodes, P for protection, R for protection-related, S for sensors, T for instrument transformers, X for switchgear, Y for power transformers, and Z for other equipment. XCBR is the circuit-breaker example developed in the paper, and MMXU is the three-phase measurement unit, with instance suffixes such as MMXU1 and MMXU2 when a device measures more than one feeder. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 4.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 4

question: A station still has legacy DNP and Modbus IEDs that must appear in the new IEC 61850 system. What modeling approach does the overview say the standard already supports for that gateway role?
choices: A single physical device can contain multiple logical devices, so a data concentrator or multi-device gateway can present each legacy IED as its own logical device without leaving the standard
IEC 61850 cannot represent legacy devices at all; they must be replaced before the station bus is commissioned
Each physical device may contain only one logical device, so a gateway is outside the model
Legacy protocols can be used only if they are first converted to GSSE
explanation: The logical-device model is well suited to legacy protocols. Support for more than one logical device inside a single physical device lets IEC 61850 model a data concentrator or a multi-device gateway directly, without techniques outside the standard. The paper also notes that OPC can be used to build a simple gateway into a substation SCADA system, so data from older devices can be reached as IEC 61850 data. Source: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 9.1.
reference: Adamiak, Baigent, and Mackiewicz, IEC 61850 Communication Networks and Systems in Substations: An Overview for Users, section 9.1
